question.text: Evaluate the surface integral \[ \displaystyle \iint\limits_{S} \dfrac{x}{x^2+y^2} \: \textrm{d}S, \] where $S$ is defined by $z=-x+\sqrt2 y$ and whose domain is the quarter-circle of radius $3$ centered at $O$ in the second quadrant, as shown above.
question.explanation:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

\[ \iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S = \iint\limits_D f\left(x,y,g(x,y)\right) \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A. \]

For the partial derivatives, we have

\[ \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(-x+\sqrt2 y) = -1, \] and \[ \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(-x+\sqrt2 y) =\sqrt2. \]

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

\begin{align*} \displaystyle \iint\limits_{S} \dfrac{x}{x^2+y^2} \: \textrm{d}S &= \iint\limits_D f\left(x,y,g(x,y)\right) \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \dfrac{x}{x^2+y^2} \cdot \sqrt{1+(-1)^2+(\sqrt2)^2}\, \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D \dfrac{x}{x^2+y^2} \cdot \sqrt{4}\, \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= 2\iint\limits_D \, \dfrac{x}{x^2+y^2}\: \text{d}A. \end{align*}

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r, \theta),$ our domain can be expressed as

\[ \Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 3, \: \dfrac{\pi}{2} \leq \theta \leq \pi \right\}. \]

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta,$ we obtain

\begin{align} 2 \iint\limits_D \, \dfrac{x}{x^2+y^2} \: \text{d}A & = 2\iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \: r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta \\[5pt] & =2 \iint\limits_{\Delta} \dfrac{r\cos\theta}{r^2\cos^2{\theta}+r^2\sin^2 \theta} \cdot r \ \textrm{d}r \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = 2 \iint\limits_{\Delta} \dfrac{r^2\cos{\theta}}{r^2(\cos^2{\theta} + \sin^2{\theta})} \: \textrm{d}r \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = 2 \iint\limits_{\Delta} \cos{\theta} \: \textrm{d}r \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = 2 \int_{0}^{3} \int_{\pi/2}^{\pi}\cos{\theta} \: \textrm{d}\theta \: \textrm{d}r \\[5pt] & = 2 \int_{0}^{3} \left[ \,\sin\theta \, \,\right ]_{\pi/2}^{\pi} \: \textrm{d} r \\[5pt] & =2 \int_0^{3} (-1) \: \textrm{d}r \\[5pt] & = 2 \cdot(-1)\cdot 3 \\[5pt] & = -6. \end{align}

question.text: Evaluate the surface integral \[ \displaystyle \iint\limits_{S} (x+y ) \: \textrm{d}S, \] where $S$ is defined by $z=-2x+2y$ and whose domain is the left half-circle of radius $1$ centered at $O$, as shown above.
question.explanation:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

\[ \iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S = \iint\limits_D f\left(x,y,g(x,y)\right) \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A. \]

For the partial derivatives, we have

\[ \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(-2x+2y) = -2, \] and \[ \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(-2x+2y) = 2. \]

Therefore, the surface integral can be expressed as follows:

\begin{align*} \displaystyle \iint\limits_{S} (x+y) \: \textrm{d}S &= \iint\limits_D f\left(x,y,g(x,y)\right) \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D (x+y)\cdot \sqrt{1+(-2)^2+2^2}\, \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D (x+y) \cdot \sqrt{9}\: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= 3 \iint\limits_D \, (x+y ) \: \text{d}A. \end{align*}

Notice that in polar coordinates $(r, \theta),$ our domain can be expressed as

\[ \Delta = \left\{ (r,\theta) \: : \: 0 \leq r \leq 1, \: \dfrac{\pi}{2} \leq \theta \leq \dfrac{3\pi}{2} \right\}. \]

Therefore, using the change of variables formula for polar coordinates, where $x=r\cos\theta$ and $y=r\sin\theta,$ we obtain

\begin{align} 3 \iint\limits_D \,(x+y)\: \text{d}A & = 3 \iint\limits_{\Delta} \ f(r\cos\theta, r\sin\theta) \: r \ \mathrm d r \mathrm d \theta \\[5pt] & =3 \iint\limits_{\Delta} (r\cos\theta + r\sin\theta ) \cdot r\,\textrm{d}r \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = 3 \iint\limits_{\Delta} r^2 (\cos\theta +\sin\theta )\: \textrm{d}r \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = 3 \int_{\pi/2}^{3\pi/2}(\cos\theta +\sin\theta )\int_{0}^{1} r^2 \: \textrm{d}r \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = 3 \int_{\pi/2}^{3\pi/2} (\cos\theta +\sin\theta) \left[ \dfrac{r^3}{3} \right ]_{0}^{1} \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = \int_{\pi/2}^{3\pi/2}( \cos\theta +\sin\theta) \: \textrm{d}\theta \\[5pt] & = \Big [ \, \sin \theta-\cos\theta \Big ]_{\pi/2}^{3\pi/2} \\[5pt] & = -2. \end{align}

question.text: Evaluate the surface integral \[ \iint\limits_{S} 4z \: \textrm{d}S \] where $S$ is defined by $z=x+y$ for $0 \leq x \leq 1$ and $0 \leq y \leq 1.$
question.explanation:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

\[ \iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S = \iint\limits_D f\left(x,y,g(x,y)\right) \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A. \]

For the partial derivatives, we have

\[ \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(x+y) = 1, \] and \[ \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(x+y) = 1. \]

Therefore, the surface integral can be evaluated as follows:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S 4z \: \textrm{d}S &= \iint\limits_D f\left(x,y,g(x,y)\right) \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D\, 4(x+y) \: \sqrt{1+1^2+1^2} \: \text{d}A\\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{1} \int_{0}^{1} 4(x+y) \sqrt{3} \: \text{d}y \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \sqrt 3 \int_{0}^{1} \left[ 4xy+2y^2 \right]_{y=0}^{y=1} \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \sqrt 3 \int_{0}^{1} (4x+2) \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \sqrt 3 \left[ 2x^2+2x \right]_{0}^{1} \\[5pt] &= 4\sqrt 3 \end{align*}

question.text: Evaluate the surface integral \[ \iint\limits_{S} (24xy + z^2) \: \textrm{d}S \] where $S$ is defined by $z=3x-4y$ for $1 \leq x \leq 2$ and $0 \leq y \leq 1.$
question.explanation:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

\[ \iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S = \iint\limits_D f\left(x,y,g(x,y)\right) \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A. \]

For the partial derivatives, we have

\[ \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x}(3x-4y) = 3, \] and \[ \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y}(3x-4y) = -4. \]

Therefore, the surface integral can be evaluated as follows:

\begin{align*} \iint\limits_S (24xy + z^2) \: \textrm{d}S &= \iint\limits_D f\left(x,y,g(x,y)\right) \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D\, \big(24xy + (3x-4y)^2\big) \sqrt{1+3^2+(-4)^2} \: \text{d}A\\[5pt] &= \sqrt{26} \iint\limits_D\, (24xy + 9x^2 + 16y^2 - 24xy) \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{26} \iint\limits_D\, (9x^2 + 16y^2) \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{26} \int_{1}^{2} \int_{0}^{1} (9x^2 + 16y^2) \: \text{d}y \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{26} \int_{1}^{2} \left[ 9x^2y + \dfrac{16}{3}y^3 \right]_{y=0}^{y=1} \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{26} \int_{1}^{2} \left(9x^2 + \dfrac{16}{3}\right) \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{26} \left[ 3x^3 + \dfrac{16}{3}x \right]_1^2 \\[5pt] &= \sqrt{26} \left( 24 + \dfrac{32}{3} - 3 - \dfrac{16}{3}\right) \\[5pt] &= \dfrac{79}{3}\sqrt{26} \end{align*}

question.text: Evaluate the surface integral \[ \iint\limits_{S} \dfrac{z}{\sqrt{1 + 2\cos^2(x+y)}} \: \textrm{d}S \] where $S$ is defined by $z=\sin(x+y)$ for $0 \leq x \leq \pi$ and $-x \leq y \leq x.$
question.explanation:
For a surface $S$ defined by $z=g(x,y)$ with $(x,y)\in D,$ the surface integral of a scalar function $f(x,y,z)$ over $S$ is given by

\[ \iint\limits_S f(x,y,z) \, \textrm{d}S = \iint\limits_D f\left(x,y,g(x,y)\right) \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A. \]

For the partial derivatives, we have

\[ \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial x} \sin(x+y) = \cos(x+y), \] and \[ \dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y} = \dfrac{\partial}{\partial y} \sin(x+y) = \cos(x+y). \]

Therefore, the surface integral can be evaluated as follows:

\begin{align*} \require{cancel} \iint\limits_S \dfrac{z}{\sqrt{1 + 2\cos^2(x+y)}} \: \textrm{d}S &= \iint\limits_D f\left(x,y,g(x,y)\right) \sqrt{1+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial x}\right)^2+\left(\dfrac{\partial z}{\partial y}\right)^2} \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D\, \dfrac{\sin(x+y)}{\sqrt{1 + 2\cos^2(x+y)}}\sqrt{1+2(\cos(x+y))^2} \: \text{d}A\\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D\, \dfrac{\sin(x+y)}{\cancel{\sqrt{1 + 2\cos^2(x+y)}}} \cancel {\sqrt{1+2(\cos(x+y))^2}}\: \text{d}A\\[5pt] &= \iint\limits_D\, \sin(x+y) \: \text{d}A \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{\pi} \int_{-x}^{x} \sin(x+y) \: \text{d}y \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \int_{0}^{\pi} \big[ -\cos(x+y) \big]_{y=-x}^{y=x} \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &=\int_{0}^{\pi} \left( 1 - \cos(2x) \right) \: \text{d}x \\[5pt] &= \left[ x - \dfrac{\sin(2x)}2 \right]_{0}^{\pi} \\[5pt] &= \pi \end{align*}
